projects.name: Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro
projects.notes:
FIRST DON’T BUY IT YET REVIEW

Working angle: “Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro: DON’T BUY IT Until You Know These 7 Things”

Research check — Oct. 2, 2026:
• Official U.S. listing: 20,000 Pa HyperForce suction.
• Official U.S. price observed: $549.99 vs $799.99 list price.
• Official features: dual anti-tangle system, auto mop detachment for carpets, reversible side brush/corner coverage, multifunction dock, app control.
• Roborock Fall Prime Day page lists $484.99 for the Oct. 6–11 main-event window. Recheck price immediately before publishing.
• Recent WIRED hands-on review praised vacuuming/mopping and corner cleaning, but reported trouble detecting cords, cat toys and other small objects; spill cleanup was a weaker area.
• Recent TechRadar testing found excellent mopping and good vacuuming, but noted the tall LiDAR limits low-furniture clearance, the dock needs floor space, disposable dust bags add running cost, and a charging cable caused trouble.

VOICE LANGUAGE RULE:
Say “I researched…”, “Roborock says…”, “WIRED found…”, “TechRadar found…”, or “reviewers reported…”. Do NOT say “I tested” because we do not own/test this unit.
projects.voiceChunks:
01. Robot vacuums have officially entered the “this is either genius or mildly terrifying” phase. They can mop your floors, empty their own dirt, and map your whole house. The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro does all of that for about five-fifty right now.

02. Before you spend that money, though, here’s the question: is this thing actually a killer value, or is it just another expensive hockey puck that eventually eats a phone charger and ruins your afternoon?

03. I’m Rock, and this is DON’T BUY IT YET — the channel where we figure out what’s worth your money before you waste it.

04. First, the good shit. Roborock gives the Qrevo 2 Pro twenty-thousand pascals of advertised suction, a dual anti-tangle brush system, spinning mop pads, edge cleaning, automatic mop removal for carpet, and a dock that handles a lot of the dirty work.

05. The auto mop removal is one of the features I actually like on paper. Instead of dragging wet mop pads across your carpet like some drunk janitor, the robot can leave the mop pads at the dock when the job calls for vacuuming carpet.

06. You also get the DuoDivide anti-tangle brush and a reversible side brush designed to work into corners. And according to independent testing, corner cleaning is one of the things this machine actually does pretty damn well.

07. WIRED liked the vacuuming, mopping, suction, controls, and corner coverage. TechRadar also came away impressed with the mopping and said overall vacuum performance was solid. So the basic job — cleaning your floors — is not where this thing falls apart.

08. The dock is another big reason people buy these. It empties debris into a disposable bag and washes the mop pads, which means less time touching whatever disgusting combination of dog hair, Cheerios, dirt, and mystery floor debris your family creates.

09. Now for the stuff the product page isn’t screaming at you.

10. Obstacle avoidance is not magic. This model uses LiDAR for navigation and structured-light sensors for obstacles. That helps it understand rooms and avoid a lot of junk, but it does not have the same kind of object recognition you get from a camera-equipped robot.

11. And that matters. Reviewers have reported problems with small items like charging cables, cat toys, and other low-profile objects. So if your floor looks like a Best Buy cable aisle exploded, don’t expect this thing to become Batman and dodge every wire.

12. That is probably the biggest practical warning with the Qrevo 2 Pro. The cleaning can be excellent, but you still need to do a quick floor check before sending it on an unsupervised mission.

13. There are some other annoyances too. The LiDAR turret makes the robot taller than the lowest-profile models, so it may not fit under every couch or cabinet. The dock also takes up real floor space, and the disposable dust bags create an ongoing cost.

14. WIRED also found spill cleanup only mediocre. So if your idea of mopping is dealing with major wet disasters every day, don’t assume spinning pads turn this thing into a miniature janitorial crew.

15. Now let’s talk about the part almost nobody talks about enough: privacy.

16. This robot learns the layout of your home. That’s literally part of how LiDAR navigation works. It also connects to an app and a cloud-connected smart-home ecosystem. So yes — there is data involved here, and pretending there isn’t would be bullshit.

17. But here’s an important distinction. On this specific Qrevo 2 Pro, Roborock’s U.S. product information does not advertise a camera, microphone, built-in voice assistant, video calling, or an audio-recording feature. It uses LiDAR and structured-light sensing.

18. So no, based on the hardware and features I could verify, this model does not look like a little rolling spy microphone waiting to record you and your wife having sex and upload the greatest hits to the cloud.

19. And I’m joking, but that is a real concern with smart-home products. If something has a microphone or camera inside your house, you should absolutely know whether it records, where that data goes, and whether those features can be shut off.

20. Roborock does make other vacuums with built-in voice assistants, cameras, pet photos, and live video features. For those models, Roborock says audio and video are not stored, voice commands are processed on-device, and live streams are encrypted.

21. The Qrevo 2 Pro is the less creepy setup because the features I could verify are about mapping and obstacle sensing, not watching or listening to the room.

22. That does not mean zero privacy risk. Your floor map, room setup, cleaning history, account information, device settings, and app connectivity are still things worth protecting.

23. And Roborock has had security problems before. In 2021, the company disclosed a vulnerability involving the Tuya IoT cloud on several older Roborock models. The exposed category of data included device information, cleaning data, maps, settings, and customization options.

24. That old vulnerability was disclosed as resolved, and those affected models were older products — not this Qrevo 2 Pro. But it proves the point: smart appliances are computers on wheels, and computers can have security flaws.

25. Roborock says it provides at least two years of security updates. I’d still use a strong unique password, keep firmware updated, and put smart-home gear on a guest or isolated Wi-Fi network if your router supports it.

26. Now back to whether this thing is actually worth buying.

27. At its roughly eight-hundred-dollar list price, I think the competition gets uncomfortable. At around five-fifty, which is where Roborock has been selling it recently, the argument gets a lot stronger.

28. You’re getting high advertised suction, excellent mopping according to reviewers, automatic mop removal, strong edge cleaning, anti-tangle hardware, self-emptying, mop washing, and a good app without stepping into the thousand-dollar-plus insanity of flagship robot vacuums.

29. But the tradeoff is clear. This thing is better at cleaning dirt than understanding every random object your family leaves on the floor.

30. If your house is reasonably tidy, you have mixed hard floors and carpet, you have pets or long hair, and you want to automate as much floor cleaning as possible, this looks like a very strong fit.

31. If you have charging cables, toys, socks, pet crap, and chaos scattered everywhere, I would think twice. Not because it can’t clean — because one bad encounter with a cord can turn your relaxing automated clean into a pain in the ass.

32. And if privacy is your number-one concern, I actually prefer that this particular model appears to skip the camera-and-microphone features found on some more expensive robots. You still have app and mapping data to think about, but that is a smaller attack surface.

33. So here’s the DON’T BUY IT YET verdict — not a score, just the stuff I’d want to know before spending my own money.

34. The Qrevo 2 Pro looks like a damn good floor cleaner at the discounted price. Its strengths are the things that actually matter every day: suction, mopping, carpet handling, corners, hair, and less maintenance.

35. Its weaknesses are also very real: weak recognition of some small obstacles, a fairly large dock, consumable bags, imperfect spill cleanup, and the normal privacy baggage that comes with putting another Wi-Fi-connected smart device inside your house.

36. If the price is around five-fifty, this one stays on my shortlist. If it jumps back to eight hundred, I’m shopping the competition before I hit buy.

37. And whatever you do, clean the damn charging cables off the floor first.

38. If you want the current price or deal, check the link in the description once we have the affiliate offer live. Subscribe if you want product reviews without the fake excitement and corporate-ass kissing. This is DON’T BUY IT YET.
